title: Weakness on both sides of the face

blocks.text: Weakness on both sides of the face

AMaC MRCP PACES · R5-170 · Neurological examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examination, at least 4 questions) · Guideline dates and links in section 15 · Related AMaC: condition may appear elsewhere in a different context

Dear Doctor, examine the face and relevant cranial nerves of a woman aged 52, whose facial weakness has persisted after an admission six months ago. Summarise the distribution, suggest causes and discuss safety. You may request relevant additional neurological findings. This is a stable follow-up examination, not an acutely deteriorating patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: A symmetrical face can still be weak on both sides.
TRAP: Calling bilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness “bilateral Bell’s palsy” closes the differential too early.

rows: “Please lift your eyebrows, close your eyes tightly and show your teeth.”
Compare forehead, eye closure and lower facial movement on each side.
“Do your eyes dry out, or does food or drink give you trouble?”
Check closure, facial sensation and relevant bulbar function.
Find the neurological company it keeps.
“I would examine limb power and reflexes as well.”
Look for a peripheral neuropathy pattern and ask about the original illness.
“A new or spreading weakness would need urgent reassessment.”
Distinguish residual deficits from recurrent acute weakness or respiratory/bulbar deterioration.
Accepts a symmetric resting face as normal.
Tests both upper and lower facial movements.
Finds bilateral weakness despite little resting asymmetry.
Tests closure gently and identifies a residual gap.
Links incomplete closure to immediate surface-care needs.
Screens eye movements, sensation and bulbar function.
Uses additional limb reflex findings to assess a wider neuropathy.
Diagnoses two idiopathic palsies without a differential.
Describes bilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness.
Integrates a preceding areflexic illness while considering infective and inflammatory alternatives.
Orders routine repeat lumbar puncture for every residual palsy.
Checks the previous diagnosis and rehabilitation plan.
Targets further tests to new evidence rather than repeating an old acute work-up.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): misses swallowing or breathing deterioration.
States acute safety triggers and eye protection.
Checks nutrition, communication and ongoing support without promising full recovery.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade.
Skills: A physical examination; B identifying physical signs; C clinical communication; D differential diagnosis; E clinical judgement; F managing patients’ concerns; G maintaining patient welfare.

Patient: a teaching assistant. Six months ago you developed tingling, then difficulty walking and facial weakness after a diarrhoeal illness. You were admitted, monitored and treated with intravenous immunoglobulin; the discharge letter says Guillain–Barré syndrome. Your walking has largely recovered, but you cannot purse your lips firmly and your eyes dry out. You have not developed new weakness, breathlessness or choking.

Only if asked: lubricating eye drops help; you use night-time eye protection as taught by the eye team. You are embarrassed when drinking in public. No tick exposure, recent travel or parotid swelling; no drug allergies. Opening: “I look almost normal, but my face does not work properly.” Do not pretend to choke or become breathless. If a candidate assumes you are fully recovered, explain that soup sometimes escapes your lips, rather than from a swallowing obstruction.

Findings and delivery. Forehead wrinkling is reduced bilaterally, eye closure is weak with small residual gaps, and cheek inflation and lip seal are weak on both sides. Facial sensation and corneal sensation, if appropriately assessed, are preserved; the candidate should not touch the cornea with an unsafe improvised object. Eye movements and pupils are normal. Voice and palate movement are normal and there is no tongue wasting or fasciculation. Additional findings on request: limb power is 5/5, deep tendon reflexes remain reduced throughout, and gait is independent. No current respiratory distress. Prior discharge summary confirms the described Guillain–Barré episode; it does not establish the cause of any future deterioration.

Question ladder. Q1 (R4) How would you describe the face? Bilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness, affecting forehead and lower-face movement. Q2 (R4) What causes would you consider? A polyneuropathy such as Guillain–Barré syndrome fits this history; consider Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV and other inflammatory/infective causes when context supports them. Q3 (R3) What further bedside information matters? Bulbar function, respiratory symptoms, limb power, reflexes and sensory findings; use formal respiratory measures in an acute neuropathic presentation. Q4 (R5) Why not diagnose bilateral Bell’s palsy? Bilateral facial weakness warrants a systemic and neurological assessment; idiopathic facial palsy should not be assumed from appearance. Q5 (R6) What if weakness starts progressing again? Arrange urgent neurological assessment, with immediate emergency review for breathing, swallowing or rapidly progressive limb symptoms; do not simply renew physiotherapy.
Examines forehead and lower face bilaterally (A B).
Recognises a peripheral rather than isolated unilateral pattern (D).
Connects residual areflexia to the previous illness (B D).
Plans eye protection and responds to new bulbar/respiratory risk (E G).
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: “Your face is symmetrical, so the nerves have recovered.” [R1 Fail] Does not test eye closure and recommends no follow-up. [R2 Fail R5 Fail]
Pass performance

CANDIDATE finds bilateral upper- and lower-face weakness, preserved facial sensation and residual areflexia. [R1 Pass R3 Pass] Gives a peripheral-neuropathy differential and protects the ocular surface. [R4 Pass R6 Pass]
High-performance performance

CANDIDATE distinguishes a poor lip seal from pharyngeal dysphagia, checks the previous discharge diagnosis and sets a clear response to genuinely new deterioration. [R3 High R5 High R6 High] EXAMINER: uses the history to interpret the signs without letting an old label explain every future symptom.
R1: Resting symmetry cannot demonstrate facial strength.
R4: Bilateral disease should widen, rather than narrow, the differential.
R6: Eye and bulbar risks remain relevant in a recovered walker.
“I need to test movement on both sides rather than judge the resting face.”
“Let me distinguish leakage at the lips from difficulty swallowing.”
“New progression would require a fresh assessment.”

A peripheral facial pattern involves the upper and lower face. Bilateral facial weakness may accompany a generalised neuropathy even when walking has recovered. The supplied history supports residual Guillain–Barré syndrome; ongoing or recurrent decline is a new clinical problem. Eye protection should follow the ophthalmic plan. NICE NG127 provides the national referral framework for rapid symmetrical neurological deterioration; it does not make this stable residual case an indication for empirical repeat immunoglobulin.
THINK: Symmetry is not normality.
SAY: “Both facial nerves appear weak.”
DO: Forehead, closure, smile, cheeks, other cranial nerves and reflexes.
NUMBERS: Six months describes this case, not an expected recovery deadline.
TRAP: Two Bell’s palsies without a systemic assessment.
FINISH: Verify the prior illness, protect eyes and define new deterioration.
